title: Your First Set
story: You're tagging photos for a gallery. A photo can be 'nature,' 'sunset,' and 'portrait' — but it shouldn't be tagged 'sunset' twice. You need a collection where duplicates just disappear.
why: Set[T] guarantees uniqueness — every element appears at most once, making it ideal for tags, categories, and membership tracking.
analogy: A Set is like a stamp collection — you can't have two of the same stamp. If you try to add a stamp you already own, it just doesn't go in. Unlike a Vec (which is like a pile of receipts where duplicates pile up), a Set automatically deduplicates everything.
try_it: Create a Set of banned usernames. Ask the user to pick a username (hardcode a test string) and check if it's banned with `.contains()`. Try inserting 10 random numbers (with some repeats) into a Set — how many unique numbers do you end up with? Convert a Vec with duplicates into a Set to see the unique count.
tips: Use Set when you need to prevent duplicates — it's simpler than checking a Map or Vec manually
`.insert()` silently ignores duplicates — no error, no crash, the Set just stays the same
`.contains()` is the main reason to use Set — membership testing is its superpower
common_mistakes: Expecting an error when inserting a duplicate — Set silently ignores duplicates, which is by design
Using Set when you need to COUNT occurrences — Set loses frequency info; use Map[Str,Int] for counting
Trying to `.get()` from a Set — Set doesn't have `.get()`; use `.contains()` and `.remove()` instead
